title: Hobby Shops In East Texas Are Buzzing With Geek Energy - NewsBreak
text:
By Puff ,
9 hours ago
Once upon a time, not all that long ago, being called a “nerd” or a “geek” was considered an insult. But, in today’s world, it seems that everyone is a nerd or geek about something. Over the last 5 years or so, “Nerd Culture” has exploded!
I mean, I’ve always been big into comic books. And I remember that some folks viewed shopping at a comic shop the same as hitting a XXX store. But now, I run into all kinds of people in shops on new Comic Book Day – from doctors to lawyers to construction workers.
Everywhere you look – there’s geeky stuff. And, everywhere you look, there’s lots of people of all kinds openly into it. And it’s great to see!
On Some Level, Everyone is a “Nerd’ or ‘Geek’ There’s comic book stores, hobby shops, conventions, and card shops popping up everywhere. Baseball cards are cool again. Comic books are cool again. Magic is cool again. It’s kind of awesome to see because there’s a little something for everyone.
If you’re into Dungeons & Dragons or table top games, there’s a place for you. If you’re super into sports, there’s a spot for you. If you love comic books and super heroes, there’s something for you.
Nerd culture is pretty much everywhere you look – even the mainstream. Annually, (generally speaking) the top grossing movies or most viewed streaming shows are either comic book or video game related.
Hobby Shops Near Lufkin, Texas Photo by João Pedro Schmitz on Unsplash Whether you’ve been buying your stuff online and would prefer to meet locals or are thinking about dipping your toes back into the world of comics, collectibles or games, believe or not, East Texas is a great place to be.
There are several high quality hobby shops of different kinds to choose – from stores that focus more on gaming to shops that lean more heavily on comic books or cards.
Some are in town, some are a short drive away. All are worth checking out!
The Chadderbox – If tabletop games or card games are your jam, the Chadderbox located in the Lufkin Mall is worth checking out. Yes, the sell comics, but the focus definitely seems to be on the gaming aspect – particularly Pokemon, Magic, and RPG games. Grim’s Fiction – Located in Nacogdoches, this may be the most unique shop on the list. Because this a bookstore…that just happens to be super Geeky. So, if you’re a reader, this is the place to check out period. They do book signings and all kinds of cool stuff. Plus, they sell tons of comics and graphic novels. And offer tabletop gaming. So, yeah, a full service shop with tons of cool stuff. Ground Zero Comics – Located in Tyler, Ground Zero is just what the name says – an old school, awesome comic book shop. Of course they sell other things like collectibles, cards, Tabletop game stuff etc., but their bread & butter are comics. Which, personally, is my jam. So, whether you want to pick up the latest run of Batman or find some books from the 60s, this is a place to check out. I’m just highlighting those 3 shops, because those are the 3 I’ve personally dealt with before and have experience with. BUT, there are tons of other cool places worth checking out all over East Texas, Dallas, Shreveport, Texarkana…basically everywhere if you look hard enough.
The point of all this – if you’re interested in comics, sports, card games, role playing games, or anything in between, there’s definitely somewhere for you to go and learn and hangout and meet people.
And that’s really what it’s all about, community and camaraderie. Who knows…you may go in to one of these places to look around and end up in a new Fantasy Football league or playing Magic on Friday nights.
20 Comic Book Movies You Forgot Existed There have been so many movies based on comics in recent years, you might not even remember all of them (or most of them). Warner Bros. Superman and the Mole Men (1951) The first Superman feature wasn’t Richard Donner’s 1978 extravaganza starring Christopher Reeve as the Man of Steel. Television’s first Clark Kent, George Reeves, actually played Superman for the first time on the big-screen, in this forgotten film that served as a kind of large-scale pilot for his The Adventures of Superman TV series. (The feature was later broken into two parts and aired as part of the Adventures of Superman syndication package.) In it, Superman doesn’t battle the Mole Men. (Spoiler alert for a 70 year old movie no one but me remembers!) Superman actually protects the Mole Men from an angry mob of small-town hicks who assume that because these little men from the center of the Earth look a little unusual that they must be “monsters.” Cinerama Releasing Tales From the Crypt (1972) Almost 20 years before the ghoulish Cryptkeeper became something of a mascot for pre- Sopranos HBO, the same twisted EC Comics series served as the inspiration for an English horror anthology also called Tales From the Crypt . Joan Collins and Peter Cushing headlined the horror film, comprised of five shorts adapted from various issues of Tales From the Crypt and its sister publication, The Vault of Horror. (A second anthology film titled The Vault of Horror followed in 1973.) ABC The Spirit (1987) Frank Miller’s disastrous Spirit film, based on the classic newspaper supplement by cartoonist Will Eisner, is already pretty obscure. But it’s practically The Dark Knight compared to the Spirit’s first adaptation, a little-seen TV film that originally aired on ABC in the summer of 1987 and starred Sam Jones — best known as Flash Gordon in the campy 1980 film about the pulp hero. Jones’ The Spirit was intended as a backdoor pilot for a full-fledged TV series, but the finished product was poorly received by ABC and aired only once. That’s despite the fact that this Spirit was written by Steven E. de Souza in his action film heyday. (The movie aired the same year as The Running Man premiered, and one year before the debut of Die Hard. ) Eisner was supposedly not happy with the results; he died in 2005 and didn’t live to see Miller’s version. Gramercy Barb Wire (1996) Barb Wire appeared in a bunch of mid-’90s comics from Dark Horse; she’s a buxom blonde bounty hunter in an dystopian version of the United States. Her look made her an ideal Pamela Anderson vehicle in her Baywatch heyday. Anderson was an undeniably striking beauty and screen presence, but her acting chops left something to be desired and the movie version was, at best, a low-budget campfest. Still, the film has its defenders; it was recently featured on the Criterion Channel in a collection of films “honored” by the Razzies. Warner Bros. Steel (1997) In between the Christopher Reeve Superman s and Superman Returns , Warner Bros. tried to relaunch the franchise in a bunch of different ways. The most famous, Superman Lives , very nearly got made with Nicolas Cage in the title role and Tim Burton behind the camera, but that film fell apart in pre-production. Somehow, Warner Bros. did make Steel , though, starring Shaquille O’Neill as one of the heroes who replaced the Man of Steel during his temporary “death” in ’90s DC comics. The movie version was the precursor to Sony’s dreadful Spider-Man “spinoffs” in which Spidey does not appear. Without the actual Superman to inspire him, Steel became a movie about a very tall man who puts on a very goofy-looking suit of armor to fight crime. Universal Virus (1999) It’s hard to believe anyone could forget a movie that contained that image of Donald Sutherland, but it happened. This one was based on a series published by Dark Horse Comics, about an alien that builds weird creatures by combining human beings and assorted technology. As you can see from the picture, the film was fairly fairly faithful to that concept. Fox From Hell (2001) Even in the vaunted career of writer Alan Moore, his graphic novel From Hell (illustrated by artist Eddie Campbell) stands as one of his greatest achievements; a rigorously researched epic tale of gothic horror set in Victorian England in the time of Jack the Ripper. Naturally, it was turned into a middling Johnny Depp detective thriller. MGM Bulletproof Monk (2003) The Bulletproof Monk Image comics were actually pretty cool. The Bulletproof Monk movie, featuring a glum Chow Yun-fat and an irritating Seann William Scott, was decidedly not cool. The only thing the movie needed to deliver were some solid action scenes, but that low bar proved impossible to clear. It may not entirely be the filmmaker’s fault, though; it looks like Scott did more of his own stunts than Chow. When Stifler is the most committed stunt performer in your action movie, you have a real problem. Lionsgate Man-Thing (2005) In the final days before Marvel launched its own film studio and became a Hollywood juggernaut, lumbering through the movie industry like a man imbued by the Crimson Gem of Cyttorak, they licensed one of their stranger creations — a mute swamp monster known as Man-Thing (no snickers, please) — to Lionsgate. Although Man-Thing was filmed as a low-budget horror release, it wound up going straight to Sci Fi Channel and then to DVD. Man-Thing eventually got a second-chance at screen stardom in a supporting role in the Disney+ special Werewolf By Night. Sony Pictures Classics Art School Confidential (2006) After director Terry Zwigoff found arthouse success directing a film version of Daniel Clowes’ Ghost World , the pair tried to conjure up another hit by adapting Clowes’ Art School Confidential to a similarly toned satire about the snoody art world. This time, critics and audiences were decidedly less enthused, and the movie failed to recoup its $5 million budget at the box office. I was a fan; I’ve always thought this is one of the great unsung dark comedies of the 2000s. If you spent time in college taking art or film classes, you will recognize a lot of truth in there. Columbia 30 Days of Night (2007) If you haunted comic-book stores in the early 2000s, you knew 30 Days of Night very well. The horror series with an irresistible high concept — an Alaskan town where it stays dark for 30 days at a time comes under attack from vampires — became a significant hit for indie publisher IDW, which then carried its story across numerous sequel books. In comic shops, surrounded by a lot of superhero stuff, 30 Days of Night really stood out. (Its striking artwork by Ben Templesmith surely helped in that regard.) In movie theaters, it became yet another vampire movie, although it did well enough to get a straight-to-video sequel based on the second 30 Days miniseries, Dark Days. Warner Bros. Whiteout (2009) Speaking of indie comic hits that got turned into a movies that were almost immediately forgotten: Whiteout ! The original book, written by Greg Rucka and illustrated by Steve Lieber, was terrific; a murder mystery set at a research station in Antarctica. (Think Sherlock Holmes meets The Thing. ) Kate Beckinsale played the central detective in the Whiteout movie, which hewed fairly close to the original concept. The film was whatever. The book is great — if you can find a copy, it’s worth a read. Warner Bros. The Losers (2010) Yep, that’s Chris Evans. Before he was Captain America (but after he was already the Human Torch) he played a member of the Losers, a team drawn from a Vertigo series loosely based on an old DC concept of the same name about an unlucky crew of World War II soldiers. The updated version featured a Special Forces team betrayed by the government who then seek revenge against the CIA. That was the basically the concept for the film version too; its very solid cast also included Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Idris Elba, and Zoe Saldana. Despite the collection of up-and-coming talent, the movie underperformed at the box office. You can still find it streaming on Max if you’re curious. Warner Bros. Jonah Hex (2010) DC Comics’ Jonah Hex is just a gruff Western vigilante with a scarred face. A movie should have been a slam dunk — just put Josh Brolin in the middle of a Fistful of Dollars -esque plot and let him be a gunslinging badass. Instead, the film inexplicably gave him supernatural powers (he can talk to the dead) and absurd, cartoonish guns to match its absurd, cartoonish plot. On the plus side, the film runs less than 90 minutes. On the down side, it’s only 80 minutes long because it’s been hacked to almost incomprehensible pieces. Summit Red (2010) For a hot minute there, Red was kind of a big deal. Based on an Homage Comics limited series by Warren Ellis and Cully Hamner, it featured Bruce Willis and a cast of older stars — including Morgan Freeman and Helen Mirren — as former secret agents who reunite for one last job. The first Red was a big enough hit that Summit quickly greenlit Red 2 , where most of the original cast reunited for another one last job. You may already see the problem with that premise; although Red 2 still grossed $148 million worldwide, that was down sharply from the first film. There was no Red 3 , although you may have seen this movie on basic cable recently. It seems to air there a lot. Universal R.I.P.D. (2013) I’ve never read the R.I.P.D. comics — which were written by Peter M. Lenkov, the creator of the recent Hawaii Five-0, MacGyver , and Magnum P.I. revivals — so I can’t speak to how faithfully the R.I.P.D. film reproduces them. But if the comics were all about hackneyed buddy cop cliches, car chases, gun fights, weird-looking ghosts, and more gun fights, then it is very faithful. Despite two big-name stars (Ryan Reynolds, who kept trying to make any kind of comic-book movie work until he hit with Deadpool ) R.I.P.D. is barely entertainment. It’s more like entertainment Tofurky, extruded out of some assembly line machine to mimic actual entertainment's appearance and texture. Focus World Term Life (2016) A fairly obscure Image Comics series served as the inspiration for this fairly obscure thriller featuring Vince Vaughn and Hailee Steinfeld. The pair play an estranged father and daughter, who bond while the former takes the latter with him on the run from some bad guys who want him dead. The movie had a rocky production — the film almost fell apart completely at one point right before shooting — and then received a tiny release in theaters and on home video. As of this writing, it holds a 0 rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Fox Searchlight Wilson (2017) I’ll be honest: I didn’t even remember this one, and I have read Daniel Clowes’ Wilson. (I already told you one of the few fans of Clowes and Terry Zwigoff’s Art School Confidential movie too.) Somehow, this one completely eluded me until just now. It stars Woody Harrelson in the title role, a middle-aged man who decides to reconnect with his ex-wife, and was directed by Craig Johnson as his follow-up The Skeleton Twins , a film I saw and liked quite a bit. But Wilson didn’t get great reviews when it premiered at the Sundance Film Festival and flopped in theaters. Warner Bros. The Kitchen (2019) Here’s a film based on a series from DC’s adult-oriented Vertigo Comics imprint about a trio of mob wives who become crime bosses in 1970s New York City. Despite the cool premise and the adaptation’s three big-name leads — Melissa McCarthy, Tiffany Haddish, and Elisabeth Moss — the film received a summer release date where it felt very out of place, and it ultimately flopped in theaters. Apparently if your comic-book movie set in Hell’s Kitchen doesn’t feature Daredevil, nerds are less interested. Sony Bloodshot (2020) After decades of various Hollywood entities trying and failing to turn the characters from ’90s comic giant Valiant into movies, one finally emerged from Sony, who cast Fast & Furious ’s Vin Diesel as Bloodshot, a deadly assassin enhanced with nanite-infused blood. And all that development, Bloodshot finally premiered ... on March 13, 2020, right as the Covid pandemic shut down movie theaters all over the world. Would Bloodshot be better remembered if it had opened under better circumstances? We’ll never know. ( But I doubt it .) The 10 Best Comic Book Movies of the Last 10 Years (2015-2024) There have been a lot of comic book movies over the last ten years. These are the best of the best. Warner Bros. 10. The Batman (2022) Batman begins again in Matt Reeves dark and intelligent thriller, which puts the detective back into DC Comics. Robert Pattison plays a Bruce Wayne just two years into his work as Gotham City’s Caped Crusader when he encounters Paul Dano’s Riddler, who is killing members of the Gotham City elite as part of a sadistic puzzle that only he Dark Knight can solve.
Other Batman films have taken the character seriously, but I’m not sure any has ever treated what the character means — to his fans as well as to the fictional residents of Gotham City — any more thoughtfully, at least until The Batman ’s rambling series of endings, which deserve comparison to The Lord of the Ring: The Return of the King. Netflix 9. Nimona (2023) While live-action superheroes tend to draw the biggest budgets and most attention, many of the best comic book adaptations in recent years are of the animated variety. Like the witty Nimona , based on the graphic novel by ND Stevenson. In the film, the title character (Chloë Grace Moretz) is a shapeshifting outsider in a quasi-futuristic medieval land who partners with another outcast (Riz Ahmed) to defeat the evildoers who have seized control of their kingdom. With an impish sense of humor, lively character animation, and a powerful message for young people about accepting themselves as they are, Nimona is an entertaining reminder that heroes come in many shapes and sizes — sometimes in a single body. Marvel 8. Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 (2023) James Gunn really stuck the landing on his Guardians of the Galaxy trilogy, with a film that provides the ideal mix of Marvel elevents: Epic action, kooky sci-fi imagery, and genuinely emotional characters we become enormously invested in. Just look at Rocket Raccoon, a D-list character who’d appeared in a handful of comics until recently, turned by Gunn in Guardians Vol. 3 into one of Marvel’s most soulful and tragic heroes. After a string of mediocre MCU titles, Gunn made capturing that old Marvel magic look easy. Too bad for Marvel fans he then jumped ship back to DC. Marvel 7. Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017) Homecoming is easily one of the most rewatchable movies in the entire Marvel Cinematic Universe. It has terrific characters, superb Spidey action, and a random street vendor asking Spider-Man to do a flip (and Spider-Man obliging). Are you not entertained?!? Tom Holland has been a real gift to Spider-Man fans; he’s great as both the quipping, flipping Spidey, and the lovelorn Peter Parker. And of all of his Marvel movies, Homecoming contains his best performance. Fox 6. Logan (2017) The third time was the charm for Hugh Jackman and solo Wolverine films. Logan finally unleashed its title character in all his bloody, tragic glory. The franchise’s first R-rating also meant a far darker, more intense adventure, one well-suited to the story of its hero’s final days. It also solved the overcrowding issue a lot of the main X-Men movies faced by stripping things down to just a few essential characters, including a superb Patrick Stewart as an aging Professor X losing his mind and therefore his control of one of the most powerful weapons on the planet. Marvel was very smart not to undo Logan ’s ending in Deadpool & Wolverine. The moment with the “X” ... that’s an incredible moment. Warner Bros. 5. The LEGO Batman Movie (2017) There was a period where my oldest daughter’s favorite film was The LEGO Batman Movie. I don’t even know how many times we watched it over a two-year period. Enough to say this: The LEGO Batman Movie is one of the most rewatchable films of the last decade. There are countless sight gags and puns and references to obscure Batman lore, plus Will Arnett’s magnificently pompous vocal performance as LEGO Batman himself. I’ve sat through a lot of kids movies over the last ten years; some amusing, some miserable. The LEGO Batman Movie is by far the funniest. And instead of mocking the character or comics, it’s a warm celebration of everything that makes the Dark Knight who he is. Marvel 4. Avengers: Endgame (2019) No superhero movie had a higher degree of difficulty than Avengers: Endgame . It had to satisfyingly resolve one of the biggest cliffhanger endings in movie history, wrap up the myriad loose plot threads of 20+ previous MCU movies, and stand alone as a satisfying piece of entertainment in its own right. Somehow, they pulled it off. Somehow, the massive pile of Easter eggs don’t get in the way of the story or the action, or the tearjerking conclusion to Robert Downey Jr.’s arc as Tony Stark. Sony 3. Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023) Expanding the vision of Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse , this ambitious sequel brings Miles Morales face-to-face with Spider-Man 2099 and his “Spider Society,” who want to protect the multiverse from “anomalies” like the Spot, a new baddie who can create interdimensional portals at will. As great as Into the Spider-Verse looked, Across the Spider-Verse looks even better and bolder. (Spider-Gwen’s world is like a watercolor painting brought to mutating life; Spider-Man India hails from a “Mumbattan” that’s a swirl of shades of yellows and greens.) The only knock against Across the Spider-Verse ? It’s the first part of a two-part story, and it does feel like it at times. Marvel 2. Black Panther (2018) Black Panther ’s utopian Wakanda already looks more poignant now than it did in 2018, for about six different reasons. The best MCU film of the last decade benefits from the presence and craftsmanship from a truly gifted director, Ryan Coogler, who built out that amazing world of Wakanda, and cast an incredible array of actors to populate it. And of course, the late Chadwick Boseman made for an incredible Black Panther, tough yet sensitive, tortured by responsibility yet resolute in his determination to protect his kingdom. Boseman’s death means we’ll never get a chance to see where King T’Challa would have gone next, or what he would have done after uniting his kingdom amidst challenges from rivals such as M’Baku (Winston Duke) and Erik “Killmonger” Stevens (Michael B. Jordan). At least we’ll have this dynamic, thrilling film to watch forever. Sony 1. Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018) Quantity rarely equals quality, but Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse really might be the most Spider-Man movie. (Or at least it was until Across the Spider-Verse arrived) as well as the best. It has a huge cast of web-slinging heroes, including young Miles Morales, brave Gwen Stacy, and depressed, middle-aged, doughy Peter B. Parker. (So relatable!) It also has maybe the most forceful and unsubtle use of Stan Lee and Steve Ditko’s moral perspective from the original Amazing Spider-Man comics of the 1960s. This film turns their concept that anyone can be a hero into a gorgeously animated celebration of their lofty ideals.
